amendments.rule: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁוַע` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **And the repeated word need not be one the source writes.** Where another rule assigns a supplied English function word to a morpheme's unit — a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object under rule 44, or a word the ASV supplies for a bare nominal under rule 33 — and the ASV writes that same word again over an elliptical or gapped parallel member, the second occurrence belongs to that same morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, however much stands between. `תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף וְכַמַּטְמוֹנִים תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה` → *search* ***for*** *her as* ***for*** *hid treasures* gives both *for*s to the verb, since the second stands for the searching the comparative clause elides, while each comparative `כְּ` takes only the *as* written for it. Do not read such a repetition as a second English word for the preposition, the conjunction or the comparative particle it stands beside, which would give one morpheme a two-word rendering the ASV writes for it nowhere else; and do not mark it `added` under rule 30, since the morpheme that licensed the first occurrence licenses this one. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the repeated word and ask whether what has gone is the reach of a rendering already placed in the clause, or a relation no morpheme there carries. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **And where the Hebrew stands the pronoun is not part of the condition.** Hebrew postposes an explicit subject pronoun after its predicate and that predicate's adjuncts, often before a coordinated second subject, while English writes a subject before its verb; where the ASV writes the pronoun in both places it has realized one written morpheme twice, and both occurrences are that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first English occurrence: `וְהִנֵּה נִצָּב עַל־עֹלָתוֹ הוּא וְכָל־שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב` → *and lo* ***he*** *was standing by his burnt offering,* ***he*** *and all the princes of Moab* gives both *he*s to the one `הוּא`, while `נִצָּב` keeps the *was standing* rule 20 leaves it and the coordinated subject keeps its own English. So read whether one written pronoun is realized twice rather than which side of the resumption it stands on, and do not hand the first occurrence to the predicate to make the units contiguous: rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing a finite verb's own person and number, and a participle or other predicate morpheme in a verbless clause takes only the copula. **And the morpheme that denotes the resumed subject need not be a pronoun.** Where a common noun or a proper name written in the verse is the referent the ASV resumes, every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first English occurrence: `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ נוֹרָא הוֹד` → ***God*** *hath upon* ***him*** *terrible majesty* gives both *God* and *him* to the one `אֱלוֹהַּ`, and `שַׁדַּי לֹא־מְצָאנֻהוּ שַׂגִּיא־כֹּחַ` → *Touching* ***the Almighty****, we cannot find him out;* ***He*** *is excellent in power* gives the resuming *He* to `שַׁדַּי`, while `שַׂגִּיא` keeps the *is excellent* rule 20 leaves it. This is the preceding paragraphs' own reasoning read for the morpheme that is actually written — the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it — since what licenses the English word is that the verse writes the referent, and not the part of speech the ASV first realized it by. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהֶּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But the morpheme those sentences look for is one the verse writes as a nominal of its own, and a finite verb's inflection is not one.** Where the only morpheme in the verse denoting that referent is the person and number of a finite verb, rule 17 has already realized it as that verb's own subject pronoun, and a further subject pronoun the ASV supplies for a coordinated verbless clause answers to nothing left in the verse: it is its own `added` unit under rule 20's closing sentence, while the copula joins the predicate as that rule directs. `יִצְפֹּן לַיְשָׁרִים תּוּשִׁיָּה מָגֵן לְהֹלְכֵי תֹם` → ***He*** *layeth up sound wisdom for the upright;* ***He*** ***is*** *a shield to them that walk in integrity* gives the first *He* to `יִצְפֹּן` under rule 17, leaves the second `added`, and puts the *is* on `מָגֵן`. Read what the verse writes rather than what the passage is about, since a referent named in a neighbouring verse is not written in this one and rule 10 makes the verse the whole unit of work; where the verse does write the nominal, the preceding paragraph governs as before. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **And where the two realizations are not of the same kind, the head goes to the one writing the noun's own lexeme, whichever of them stands first.** The direction to head on the first English occurrence settles a tie between realizations of one kind — two *he*s, two *from*s, or a noun and the pronoun resuming it in that order — and it is not a preference for the phrase's left edge. Where the ASV realizes one written nominal both by a pronoun and by the word that writes its lexeme, rule 24 governs and the head is the lexeme-bearing word, exactly as rule 18 heads a twice-written suffix on the pronoun that realizes it directly rather than on the generic noun beside it, and as rule 31 keeps a head off a word the ASV supplied. This reaches a construct chain whose *nomen rectum* the ASV promotes to the clause's English subject while writing the chain's own relation as a possessive on the head noun: `בְּפֶה חָנֵף יַשְׁחִת רֵעֵהוּ` → *With* ***his*** *mouth* ***the godless man*** *destroyeth his neighbor* gives both *his* and *the godless man* to the one `חָנֵף`, headed on *godless*, while `פֶּה` keeps its own *mouth*, and `וּבְהַוַּת בֹּגְדִים יִלָּכֵדוּ` → *But* ***the treacherous*** *shall be taken in* ***their own*** *iniquity* divides the same way, headed on *treacherous*. Such a possessive is not `added` under rule 18's closing sentence and the promoted subject is not `added` under rule 17: a morpheme in the phrase answers to each, which is the count the paragraph above runs. Read which English word writes the lexeme before reaching for the first occurrence, since Hebrew writes the possessor after its head noun while English writes the possessive before it, so the pronoun stands first as often as not. **But an expletive the ASV writes to fill a subject slot English cannot leave empty realizes no referent at all, whatever the verse writes.** Where the ASV extraposes a clausal subject the Hebrew writes — an infinitive phrase, or another clause the ASV renders in full further on — and puts an anticipatory *it* where that subject would stand, the pronoun denotes nothing the verse names and rule 20 governs it: it is its own `added` unit, while the predicate keeps the copula that rule gives it and the extraposed clause keeps its own English. `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → ***it*** *is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* leaves that *it* `added`, with *is an abomination* on the construct noun and *to depart* on the infinitive. What the sentences above place is a pronoun denoting a referent the verse names and the ASV has rendered by a word of its own, so read what the pronoun stands for before folding it into a written morpheme's unit: `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh,* ***it*** *is a tree of life* gives its *it* to `תַּאֲוָה`, which the ASV has already written as *the desire*, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 do. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once in the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amendments.why: PRO.2.4 met a case rule 25 states only for a source function word. The ASV supplies a valency preposition for `תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה` under rule 44 and writes it again inside the elliptical comparative — *search for her as for hid treasures* — and the verse pass, finding no rule for the repetition, gave the second word to the comparative `כְּ` as *as for*, inventing a two-word rendering of a particle the corpus renders *as*. The added paragraph extends the distributed reading to a supplied word another rule has already placed, on the same reasoning rule 33 uses for a written preposition rewritten over a coordinated member and rule 34 for a gapped verb's second realization. The second addition closes the gap PRO.2.7 exposed at the other end of the rule: the paragraph saying the resumed subject's morpheme need not be a pronoun reads naturally as reaching a finite verb's inflection, which would fold a second supplied *He* into a verb that rule 17 has already given one, against the rule's own count of realizations against the morphemes that could carry them. Both are qualifications of rule 25's own sentences, so they replace that rule rather than standing as new ones.

conventions: An English function word another rule has already assigned to a morpheme's unit — here the *for* rule 44 gives `תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה` to reach its bare object suffix — is given to that same morpheme again where the ASV repeats it over an elliptical parallel member: *search* ***for*** *her as* ***for*** *hid treasures* is one discontinuous verb unit, and each comparative `כְּ` keeps only the *as* written for it. Do not read the repeated word as a second word for the particle standing beside it.

`דֶּרֶךְ רָע` is tagged Ncbsa + Aamsa by MACULA — an absolute noun with an absolute modifier — so its supplied *the* is rule 15's determiner on the noun and its supplied *of* is rule 33's word for what the bare nominal contributes, not rules 29 and 19. The visually parallel `דַרְכֵי־חֹשֶׁךְ` (2.13) and `דֶרֶךְ טוֹבִים` (2.20) are construct chains and take rules 29 and 19. The morphology, not the English, decides which of the two a phrase is.

The supplied *He* opening the second colon is `added`. The only morpheme in the verse denoting that referent is `יִצְפֹּן`'s own person and number, which rule 17 has already realized as the first *He*; rule 25's distributed reading of a resumed subject rests on a written pronoun, noun or name, and a finite verb's inflection standing under a pronoun of its own is not one. The supplied *is* beside it is different — that is rule 20's construction-supplied copula and joins the nominal predicate `מָגֵן`.

`תּוּשִׁיָּה` → *sound wisdom* heads on *wisdom*. Rule 31's subtraction test ties here, and the tie is broken by the chapter's own usage: the ASV writes a bare *wisdom* for `חׇכְמָה` at 2.2, 2.6 and 2.10, which makes *wisdom* the class noun and *sound* the ASV's specifier. `תַּהְפֻּכוֹת` → *perverse things* (2.12) is the other case and heads on *perverse*, because *things* is a generic the ASV never writes alone for that word.

amended.text: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁוַע` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **And the repeated word need not be one the source writes.** Where another rule assigns a supplied English function word to a morpheme's unit — a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object under rule 44, or a word the ASV supplies for a bare nominal under rule 33 — and the ASV writes that same word again over an elliptical or gapped parallel member, the second occurrence belongs to that same morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, however much stands between. `תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף וְכַמַּטְמוֹנִים תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה` → *search* ***for*** *her as* ***for*** *hid treasures* gives both *for*s to the verb, since the second stands for the searching the comparative clause elides, while each comparative `כְּ` takes only the *as* written for it. Do not read such a repetition as a second English word for the preposition, the conjunction or the comparative particle it stands beside, which would give one morpheme a two-word rendering the ASV writes for it nowhere else; and do not mark it `added` under rule 30, since the morpheme that licensed the first occurrence licenses this one. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the repeated word and ask whether what has gone is the reach of a rendering already placed in the clause, or a relation no morpheme there carries. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **And where the Hebrew stands the pronoun is not part of the condition.** Hebrew postposes an explicit subject pronoun after its predicate and that predicate's adjuncts, often before a coordinated second subject, while English writes a subject before its verb; where the ASV writes the pronoun in both places it has realized one written morpheme twice, and both occurrences are that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first English occurrence: `וְהִנֵּה נִצָּב עַל־עֹלָתוֹ הוּא וְכָל־שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב` → *and lo* ***he*** *was standing by his burnt offering,* ***he*** *and all the princes of Moab* gives both *he*s to the one `הוּא`, while `נִצָּב` keeps the *was standing* rule 20 leaves it and the coordinated subject keeps its own English. So read whether one written pronoun is realized twice rather than which side of the resumption it stands on, and do not hand the first occurrence to the predicate to make the units contiguous: rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing a finite verb's own person and number, and a participle or other predicate morpheme in a verbless clause takes only the copula. **And the morpheme that denotes the resumed subject need not be a pronoun.** Where a common noun or a proper name written in the verse is the referent the ASV resumes, every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first English occurrence: `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ נוֹרָא הוֹד` → ***God*** *hath upon* ***him*** *terrible majesty* gives both *God* and *him* to the one `אֱלוֹהַּ`, and `שַׁדַּי לֹא־מְצָאנֻהוּ שַׂגִּיא־כֹּחַ` → *Touching* ***the Almighty****, we cannot find him out;* ***He*** *is excellent in power* gives the resuming *He* to `שַׁדַּי`, while `שַׂגִּיא` keeps the *is excellent* rule 20 leaves it. This is the preceding paragraphs' own reasoning read for the morpheme that is actually written — the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it — since what licenses the English word is that the verse writes the referent, and not the part of speech the ASV first realized it by. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהֶּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But the morpheme those sentences look for is one the verse writes as a nominal of its own, and a finite verb's inflection is not one.** Where the only morpheme in the verse denoting that referent is the person and number of a finite verb, rule 17 has already realized it as that verb's own subject pronoun, and a further subject pronoun the ASV supplies for a coordinated verbless clause answers to nothing left in the verse: it is its own `added` unit under rule 20's closing sentence, while the copula joins the predicate as that rule directs. `יִצְפֹּן לַיְשָׁרִים תּוּשִׁיָּה מָגֵן לְהֹלְכֵי תֹם` → ***He*** *layeth up sound wisdom for the upright;* ***He*** ***is*** *a shield to them that walk in integrity* gives the first *He* to `יִצְפֹּן` under rule 17, leaves the second `added`, and puts the *is* on `מָגֵן`. Read what the verse writes rather than what the passage is about, since a referent named in a neighbouring verse is not written in this one and rule 10 makes the verse the whole unit of work; where the verse does write the nominal, the preceding paragraph governs as before. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **And where the two realizations are not of the same kind, the head goes to the one writing the noun's own lexeme, whichever of them stands first.** The direction to head on the first English occurrence settles a tie between realizations of one kind — two *he*s, two *from*s, or a noun and the pronoun resuming it in that order — and it is not a preference for the phrase's left edge. Where the ASV realizes one written nominal both by a pronoun and by the word that writes its lexeme, rule 24 governs and the head is the lexeme-bearing word, exactly as rule 18 heads a twice-written suffix on the pronoun that realizes it directly rather than on the generic noun beside it, and as rule 31 keeps a head off a word the ASV supplied. This reaches a construct chain whose *nomen rectum* the ASV promotes to the clause's English subject while writing the chain's own relation as a possessive on the head noun: `בְּפֶה חָנֵף יַשְׁחִת רֵעֵהוּ` → *With* ***his*** *mouth* ***the godless man*** *destroyeth his neighbor* gives both *his* and *the godless man* to the one `חָנֵף`, headed on *godless*, while `פֶּה` keeps its own *mouth*, and `וּבְהַוַּת בֹּגְדִים יִלָּכֵדוּ` → *But* ***the treacherous*** *shall be taken in* ***their own*** *iniquity* divides the same way, headed on *treacherous*. Such a possessive is not `added` under rule 18's closing sentence and the promoted subject is not `added` under rule 17: a morpheme in the phrase answers to each, which is the count the paragraph above runs. Read which English word writes the lexeme before reaching for the first occurrence, since Hebrew writes the possessor after its head noun while English writes the possessive before it, so the pronoun stands first as often as not. **But an expletive the ASV writes to fill a subject slot English cannot leave empty realizes no referent at all, whatever the verse writes.** Where the ASV extraposes a clausal subject the Hebrew writes — an infinitive phrase, or another clause the ASV renders in full further on — and puts an anticipatory *it* where that subject would stand, the pronoun denotes nothing the verse names and rule 20 governs it: it is its own `added` unit, while the predicate keeps the copula that rule gives it and the extraposed clause keeps its own English. `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → ***it*** *is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* leaves that *it* `added`, with *is an abomination* on the construct noun and *to depart* on the infinitive. What the sentences above place is a pronoun denoting a referent the verse names and the ASV has rendered by a word of its own, so read what the pronoun stands for before folding it into a written morpheme's unit: `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh,* ***it*** *is a tree of life* gives its *it* to `תַּאֲוָה`, which the ASV has already written as *the desire*, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 do. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once in the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amended.why: PRO.2.4 met a case rule 25 states only for a source function word. The ASV supplies a valency preposition for `תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה` under rule 44 and writes it again inside the elliptical comparative — *search for her as for hid treasures* — and the verse pass, finding no rule for the repetition, gave the second word to the comparative `כְּ` as *as for*, inventing a two-word rendering of a particle the corpus renders *as*. The added paragraph extends the distributed reading to a supplied word another rule has already placed, on the same reasoning rule 33 uses for a written preposition rewritten over a coordinated member and rule 34 for a gapped verb's second realization. The second addition closes the gap PRO.2.7 exposed at the other end of the rule: the paragraph saying the resumed subject's morpheme need not be a pronoun reads naturally as reaching a finite verb's inflection, which would fold a second supplied *He* into a verb that rule 17 has already given one, against the rule's own count of realizations against the morphemes that could carry them. Both are qualifications of rule 25's own sentences, so they replace that rule rather than standing as new ones.

report: One genuine split, in PRO.2.4: the verse's two comparative `כְּ`s were analysed two ways with nothing in the source licensing the difference. The first took a bare *as*, the second *as for*. But the verse had already placed that *for* — the ASV reaches `חָפַשׂ`'s bare object suffix through a supplied preposition under rule 44 (t009, *search for her*), and the elliptical comparative simply repeats that supplied word: *as for hid treasures* is *as [thou searchest] for hid treasures*. The patch gives both *for*s to the verb as one discontinuous unit and leaves each `כְּ` the *as* written for it, which also removes an unattested two-word rendering of a comparative particle.

Checked and cleared as context-licensed rather than splits: `לְ` before an infinitive (*So as to* / *To* / *That* / *to*, each what the ASV wrote); `הַ` on a substantival adjective (2.7 takes a written *the*, 2.13/2.14/2.17 take a written relative, which is rule 41's own closing direction); `וְ` → *And* / *But* (rule 14's open list); `מִן` → *Out of* in 2.6 against a bare *of* in 2.22, where *out* is the particle of the ASV's phrasal *root out* and the same verse's first colon divides identically (*cut off* / *from*); and `מִשְׁפָּט`, `אֹרַח`, `דֶּרֶךְ`, `רַע`, `טוֹב`, `שָׁמַר`, `נָצַר`, `צָפַן`, `הוּא`, which differ only where the ASV's own words differ.

Ran the `added` audit the lemma table is blind to. The seven `added` units are consistent with each other. A coordinating *And* at a second colon's head is `added` in 2.2, 2.3 and 2.14, each of which writes no waw, while all eleven written waws take the connective written for them; the *yea* of 2.9 is marked on the same count, while the `כִּי` of 2.3 takes its own *Yea*. The supplied relative is `added` in 2.16 over a finite `הֶחֱלִיקָה` but placed on the participle in 2.12 under rule 41 — a source difference, not a split.

Supplied determiners and supplied prepositions are placed by one consistent test throughout: rule 29 where MACULA writes a construct chain (2.5, 2.8, 2.13, 2.14, 2.17, 2.19, 2.20), rule 46 where the word is an anarthrous substantival adjective or participle (2.16, 2.18, 2.20, 2.21, 2.22), rule 15 where an absolute noun stands with an absolute modifier (2.12, 2.21, 2.22), and rule 33 for a supplied preposition on a bare nominal (2.12, 2.15, 2.21). The visually parallel `דֶּרֶךְ רָע` of 2.12 and `דֶרֶךְ טוֹבִים` of 2.20 divide differently only because MACULA tags the first absolute and the second construct; that is recorded as a convention.

BSB: the one disagreement is the paragogic nun of PRO.2.19 (`יְשׁוּבוּן`), which the ASV alignment marks `unrepresented` and BSB attaches to its host word. That is rule 32 verbatim and the documented convention difference the rule names, not an error. Nothing was changed for it.

One judgment left standing rather than churned, and recorded in the log instead: the supplied *He* of 2.7's second colon is `added`. Rule 25's distributed reading places a resumed subject pronoun on a written pronoun, noun or name; here the only morpheme in the verse denoting the referent is `יִצְפֹּן`'s own inflection, which rule 17 has already given the first *He*, and rule 20's closing sentence marks the surplus. The competing reading is defensible and is named in the verse's notes.
